summary:
Nunavut is a territory of Canada and stands under the national human-rights and criminal law framework, which applies there as elsewhere in the country. Its own legislation adds a separate territorial layer.

The Nunavut Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression. Bill 31, which added both grounds alongside sexual orientation, passed third and final reading in the Legislative Assembly on 13 March 2017 with unanimous support. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. Nine provinces and one territory already listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights legislation at that point, making Nunavut the first Canadian territory to do so.

Nunavut birth certificates carry a third, non-binary sex designation. On 18 September 2025 MLAs voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore that option through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck it from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill; the bill then passed third reading. Sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals. The eight-vote minority against restoration shows the marker was contested in the legislature rather than adopted by consensus.

Transition-related surgical care funded by the territorial government is delivered through a contracted clinic in Montreal rather than at a Nunavut facility. A visitor who needs such care while in the territory would have to travel outside it.
tangentialFactors: Nunavut was the last Canadian province or territory to legalise adoption by same-sex couples, in 2011. The change is a family-recognition matter rather than a visitor-facing rule, but it marks how recently family law in the territory moved.
localsOnly: The Health Department funds transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. Breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty are named as covered procedures. The arrangement dates from March 2022, when the department began funding the care. Positive Space, a local LGBTQ organisation, called the move overdue and flagged information gaps for residents outside Iqaluit.
outOfScopeNotes:
No hate-crime reporting figures specific to Nunavut were identified in the source inventory. The national police-reported hate-crime series does not disaggregate to the territory in the material reviewed, and the national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation analysis drawn on here supplies no territorial data.

No Nunavut-specific record of enforcement action, trans-specific violence, police conduct, or screening and entry practice was identified. Whether the territorial human-rights complaint route has produced decisions involving gender identity or gender expression is not sourced.
